# fastglm

*fastglm* fits generalized linear models using C++ and RcppEigen. It accepts formulas or predictor matrices and provides methods for data held in ordinary memory, stored sparsely, accessed from a file, or read in blocks as needed.

The development version also includes negative-binomial, hurdle, zero-inflated, zero-truncated, and two-part binomial/Gamma models. New interfaces and numerical changes are described in [NEWS](NEWS.md).

## Installation

```{r, eval=FALSE}
install.packages("fastglm")               # released version
pak::pak("jaredhuling/fastglm")           # development version
```

## Fit and predict

```{r}
library(fastglm)
set.seed(1)
d <- data.frame(x=rnorm(300),exposure=runif(300,.5,2))
d$y <- rpois(300,d$exposure*exp(.2+.4*d$x))
fit <- fastglm(y~x+offset(log(exposure)),data=d,family=poisson(),method="auto")
coef(fit)
predict(fit,newdata=d[1:3,],type="response",se.fit=TRUE)
```

A prebuilt design matrix can be passed as `fastglm(X, y, family)`. The fitting method also works through `glm(..., method=fastglm_fit)`.

`method="auto"` rescales predictor columns and selects a numerical method for the weighted regressions used during fitting. It first attempts Cholesky, then uses pivoted QR if it detects redundant or nearly redundant predictors. Both are matrix decompositions: ways of arranging the regression calculation to obtain a solution. The six explicit methods remain available by name or integer. Sparse and file-backed designs use Cholesky and require that each coefficient can be estimated separately from the others.

## Inference and repeated fits

Model methods include `summary()`, `vcov()`, `predict()`, `hatvalues()`, `confint()`, and `simulate()`. Formula fits retain the information needed to reconstruct factors, contrasts, and offsets. Optional broom methods provide tidy coefficient and model summaries.

```{r}
vcov(fit,type="HC1")
fastglm_average(fit)
fastglm_diagnostics(fit)[c("converged","solver","standardized.score")]
```

`fastglm_vcov()` calculates robust standard errors, including standard errors for observations correlated within independent groups. It processes predictor rows in blocks to limit working memory. `fastglm_prepare()` and `fastglm_batch()` reuse a common predictor design across outcomes. Gaussian identity fits reuse the matrix decomposition because it depends only on predictors and weights. With `firth=TRUE`, dense Gaussian-identity, Gamma-log, and Poisson-square-root batches can also reuse their decomposition and bias-adjustment setup when the default automatic solver or `"llt"` is selected. The `workers` argument allows independent fits to run concurrently in separate R processes.

`inference="none"` skips the final covariance calculation. `retain.data=FALSE` omits the design and response from the returned object; methods that require them then need new data or a refit.

## Large data

`fastglm_streaming()` fits a model by repeatedly reading manageable blocks of observations. A supplied function, called a callback, returns the rows requested by the fitting routine. `fastglm_source()` records this function and the formula information needed to keep factor coding and transformations consistent across blocks. Optional Arrow and DBI functions read blocks from Parquet files or database queries. Each read must return the same observations in the same order throughout fitting and inference.

Prediction normally collects its results into a single vector. If that vector would be too large, the `sink` argument accepts a function that receives one block of results at a time and saves or summarizes it. This avoids keeping every prediction in memory. Robust covariance and average predictions also reread the source, retaining block-sized data, coefficient-sized summaries, and small records of block sizes. Clustered inference additionally stores a contribution vector for each group.

## Additional response models

| Function | Model |
|:--|:--|
| `fastglm_nb()` | Negative-binomial regression with estimated theta |
| `fastglm_hurdle()` | Binary positive-outcome model and truncated Poisson/NB counts |
| `fastglm_zi()` | Zero-inflated Poisson/NB counts |
| `fastglm_truncated()` | Positive counts conditional on exceeding zero |
| `fastglm_twopart()` | Binary positive-outcome model and positive Gamma outcomes |

Count-model predictions distinguish the overall response mean, the probability of observing zero, and the mean described by each model component. Prediction standard errors combine uncertainty from the relevant fitted parameters, including the negative-binomial size parameter theta. `fastglm_confint_theta()` calculates an interval by varying theta and refitting the other coefficients, a procedure called profile likelihood.

`firth=TRUE` adjusts the estimating equations to reduce small-sample mean bias for the supported standard likelihood families. Gamma fitting also adjusts estimation of dispersion, which controls variation around the fitted mean. For dense binomial-logit Firth fits, `confint(fit, method="profile")` calculates profile penalized-likelihood intervals, and `fastglm_profile_test()` tests specified coefficient values jointly. These procedures support independent binomial counts and frequency weights and use an asymptotic chi-square reference. The bias-reduction vignette explains the adjustment, inference assumptions, and numerical diagnostics.

## Documentation and benchmarks

The vignettes cover [estimation and inference](vignettes/fastglm-overview.Rmd), [large data](vignettes/large-data-fastglm.Rmd), [count models](vignettes/count-firth-fastglm.Rmd), [semicontinuous outcomes](vignettes/semicontinuous-fastglm.Rmd), and [bias reduction](vignettes/firth-fastglm.Rmd).

`benchmarks/benchmark.R` runs accuracy-checked timing comparisons and records the R session. Performance depends on family, design dimensions, conditioning, decomposition, and requested inference. The static benchmark vignettes retain their original measurement dates; they are not measurements of every subsequent development change.
